title: Your Child’s Rebellion Is Not Proof You Failed—and Their Obedience Is Not Proof You Succeeded
paragraphs: Your Child’s Rebellion Is Not Proof You Failed—and Their Obedience Is Not Proof You Succeeded
The Bible gives parents a sacred responsibility—but it never gives us permission to take either total blame or total credit for another human soul.
There is a mother reading this who has replayed the same question so many times that it has almost become a form of self-punishment.
Where did I go wrong?
She remembers the bedtime prayers.
The children’s Bible with the worn corners.
The whispered prayers beside a sleeping child who never knew how many tears fell onto that pillow.
She remembers Sunday mornings when getting everyone dressed felt like spiritual warfare before they ever reached the church parking lot.
She remembers correcting attitudes. Teaching forgiveness. Saying no when saying yes would have been easier. Apologizing when she herself was wrong.
She remembers praying over that child before school.
Before graduation.
Before they drove away.
And now that child wants almost nothing to do with God.
Maybe they walked away from church.
Maybe they are living in open rebellion.
Maybe they mock the faith they were taught.
Maybe they have made choices you never imagined they would make.
Maybe your relationship has become painfully distant.
And somewhere between their decisions and your unanswered prayers, you began conducting a trial inside your own heart.
The defendant is you.
The prosecutor is you.
The witness is every parenting mistake you can remember.
And the sentence sounds something like this:
If I had been a better parent, my child would still be walking with God.
But before you pronounce yourself guilty of something Scripture has not charged you with, you need to hear what God actually says.
And before the parent whose children are walking faithfully with Christ becomes too confident that their children's obedience proves they did everything right, they need to hear it too.
Because the same truth that can release one parent from crushing guilt can rescue another parent from quiet pride.
Ezekiel 18:20 contains words that may initially sound severe, but hidden inside their severity is a profound truth about human responsibility:
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die.”
The Hebrew begins:
הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת
Ha-nefesh ha-chotet hi tamut.
Literally, the person—the nephesh—who sins is the one who bears responsibility.
Then comes the line every guilt-ridden parent needs to sit with:
בֵּן לֹא־יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֹן הָאָב
Ben lo-yissa ba'avon ha'av.
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”
And then Scripture turns the statement around:
“Neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.”
That sentence does not mean parents have no influence.
It does not mean parental sin cannot wound children.
It does not mean generational patterns are imaginary.
It does not mean fathers and mothers can neglect, abuse, provoke, abandon, or spiritually starve their children and then shrug, “Their choices aren't my responsibility.”
Absolutely not.
Scripture takes parenting far too seriously for that.
But Ezekiel destroys another dangerous idea:
that one human being automatically carries the moral guilt of another person's choices.
Your child is your child.
Your child is not your puppet.
Your child is not your spiritual report card.
Your child is not a trophy proving your righteousness.
And your child is not automatically evidence proving your failure.
Your child is a human soul standing before God.
That changes everything.
Because Christian parents sometimes unknowingly begin believing in a formula.
Teach them Scripture.
Pray with them.
Discipline them correctly.
Homeschool them—or send them to the right Christian school.
Keep them away from certain influences.
Find the right church.
Monitor the phone.
Choose the right friends.
Have family devotions.
Do all the correct things...
and faithful Christian adulthood will come out the other side.
Then Proverbs 22:6 gets placed over the formula like a divine warranty:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”
But Proverbs are wisdom sayings, not mechanical contracts by which human beings can force predetermined spiritual outcomes from other human beings.
If Proverbs 22:6 meant that faithful parenting guaranteed faithful adult children without exception, something would become deeply confused about human responsibility.
Parents would effectively possess the ability to guarantee another person's repentance.
But Scripture never gives parents that power.
Only God changes hearts.
Only Christ saves sinners.
Only the Holy Spirit gives spiritual life.
Parents can teach truth.
Parents can model repentance.
Parents can establish boundaries.
Parents can discipline.
Parents can pray.
Parents can confess their failures.
Parents can demonstrate what forgiveness looks like.
Parents can bring children repeatedly beneath the sound of the Gospel.
Parents can plant.
Parents can water.
But there is something parents cannot do.
They cannot resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
Paul wrote:
ἐγὼ ἐφύτευσα, Ἀπολλῶς ἐπότισεν, ἀλλὰ ὁ Θεὸς ηὔξανεν.
Egō ephyteusa, Apollōs epotisen, alla ho Theos ēuxanen.
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.”
Paul was speaking about Gospel ministry, not specifically parenting, so we should not pretend the verse was originally written as parenting advice.
But the theological principle should humble every person who disciples another human being.
We labor faithfully.
God gives life and growth.
That means faithful parenting matters enormously without making parents sovereign.
Read that again.
Faithful parenting matters enormously without making parents sovereign.
Somebody reading this has spent years confusing those two things.
You were responsible to raise your child faithfully.
You were never given the power to become their Holy Spirit.
And perhaps you did fail in significant ways.
We should not soften that possibility merely because it hurts.
Maybe you were harsh.
Maybe work always came first.
Maybe your child heard you preach grace while watching you refuse to apologize.
Maybe church became a performance.
Maybe your anger frightened them.
Maybe your marriage filled their childhood with wounds.
Maybe you disciplined behavior but rarely shepherded the heart.
Maybe you demanded respect while refusing to listen.
Maybe you were physically present but emotionally absent.
Maybe they watched a public Christianity that contradicted the private atmosphere of your home.
If God is bringing something specific to your conscience, do not hide behind Ezekiel 18.
Repent.
Not vaguely.
Specifically.
Go to your child if appropriate and say what Christian parents sometimes find terrifying to say:
“I sinned against you. I was wrong. I cannot undo what happened, and I will not excuse it. Will you forgive me?”
Because Ephesians 6:4 does not merely speak to children.
It turns toward fathers:
Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἀλλὰ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ Κυρίου.
“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
Notice the balance.
There is discipline.
There is instruction.
There is nurture.
And there is a warning against provoking them.
Biblical parenting is neither passive permissiveness nor authoritarian domination.
It is stewardship beneath the lordship of Christ.
So if you sinned, repent.
If restitution is possible, pursue it.
If reconciliation is possible, seek it patiently.
If your child needs to hear an apology without immediately being handed a sermon afterward, give the apology and resist the urge to control their response.
But then...
after you have honestly faced what belongs to you...
stop trying to repent for what belongs to them.
That may be one of the hardest sentences a Christian parent ever accepts.
Your repentance cannot substitute for theirs.
Your faith cannot substitute for theirs.
Your baptism cannot substitute for theirs.
Your church attendance cannot substitute for theirs.
Your tears cannot substitute for theirs.
Your obedience cannot substitute for theirs.
Every child eventually stands before God as something more than somebody's son or somebody's daughter.
They stand before Him as a person.
And that truth works in the opposite direction too.
Maybe your children love Jesus.
Maybe they serve faithfully.
Maybe people compliment your family.
Maybe someone has told you, “You raised them right.”
Receive encouragement gratefully.
But hold the applause loosely.
Because their faithfulness does not mean you discovered the parenting formula everyone else somehow missed.
There may be another mother in your church who prayed as desperately as you did.
Another father who opened the same Bible.
Another family who attended church faithfully.
Another parent who cried over the same promises.
Their child wandered.
Yours didn't.
Be very careful what conclusion you draw from that.
The parent of an obedient child can become proud for exactly the same theological reason the parent of a rebellious child becomes crushed:
both can assume they were ultimately responsible for producing the outcome.
One says, “Look what I accomplished.”
The other says, “Look what I destroyed.”
Grace interrupts both sentences.
God says, in effect:
You were a steward.
You were not God.
That does not diminish parenting.
It makes parenting worship.
You obey because Christ is worthy—not because obedience gives you control over another person's future.
You teach because truth matters.
You discipline because love matters.
You pray because God hears.
You confess because humility matters.
You model repentance because your children need to know that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fail.
And then you entrust what you cannot control to the One who can reach places inside your child's heart that you cannot enter.
Perhaps this is where the story becomes unbearably personal.
Because your child may be far away right now.
Far from church.
Far from Scripture.
Far from the person you remember tucking into bed.
Maybe you still have their childhood Bible somewhere.
Maybe their handwriting is inside it.
Maybe there is a verse underlined by a hand that later pushed faith away.
And you sometimes open it when nobody is watching.
You remember the little voice that once prayed beside you.
Then you look at who they have become and wonder whether that little child is gone forever.
Christian parent...
you do not know the final chapter.
Do not confuse today with forever.
The father in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son knew what it meant to watch a beloved child walk deliberately away.
The son left.
The son squandered.
The son sinned.
The father did not travel into the distant country to participate in his rebellion.
He did not rename rebellion as authenticity to make separation hurt less.
But neither did he nail the door shut.
And when the son finally came home broken, the father ran.
That parable ultimately reveals something magnificent about the welcome of God toward repentant sinners.
And that is where every Christian parent's deepest hope must finally rest.
Not in perfect parenting.
Not in controlling outcomes.
Not in religious nostalgia.
Not even in the strength of your prayers.
In the mercy of God revealed through Jesus Christ.
Because there is a deeper problem than rebellious children.
There are rebellious humans.
All of us.
The scandal is not merely that some children leave the Father's house.
The scandal is that, spiritually speaking, humanity has.
We have all wanted God's gifts while resisting God's authority.
We have all sinned.
We have all wandered.
Some rebellion happens in distant countries.
Some rebellion sits obediently in church pews.
Some prodigals smell like the pigpen.
Others wear Christian clothing, know Christian vocabulary, behave beautifully, and secretly trust their own goodness.
That is why an obedient child needs Jesus just as desperately as a rebellious one.
Good behavior cannot crucify sin.
Christian parenting cannot atone for sin.
Family heritage cannot justify a sinner.
Only Jesus can save.
At the cross, Christ did what no father or mother could ever do for their child.
He bore sin.
He satisfied justice.
He opened the way home.
And in His resurrection, death did not get the final word.
That means the Gospel speaks both to the parent drowning in guilt and the parent quietly intoxicated by pride.
To the guilty parent:
Repent for what is yours.
Then bring your condemnation to Christ.
To the proud parent:
Give thanks for every evidence of grace.
Then give the glory to God.
To the parent of the prodigal:
Keep praying.
Keep loving.
Keep your convictions.
Keep your heart tender.
Do not enable destruction in the name of love.
Do not manipulate in the name of concern.
Do not compromise truth because you are terrified of losing them.
And do not declare someone beyond the reach of Christ while breath remains in their lungs.
You are looking at one chapter.
God sees the book.
Perhaps your child's rebellion has already become the place where God is exposing something in you too.
The need to control.
The need to appear successful.
The fear of what church people think.
The secret belief that if your children turned out well, it would prove something about you.
Sometimes God loves parents enough to dismantle the idol of the perfect Christian family.
Not because family faithfulness is unimportant.
But because Jesus must be more precious than the image of having raised impressive children.
And perhaps that sentence hurts.
Let it.
Then let grace reach the wound.
Your identity was never supposed to be “parent of successful Christian children.”
Your deepest identity is found in Christ.
And your child's deepest need is not to restore your reputation.
It is to be reconciled to God.
So pray differently.
Not merely:
“God, make my child behave again.”
Pray:
“Jesus, reveal Yourself to them.”
Not merely:
“Make them come back to church.”
Pray:
“Bring them to repentance and living faith.”
Not merely:
“Make them become the person they used to be.”
Pray:
“Make them new.”
And while you pray for God to work in them, invite Him to continue working in you.
Maybe there are apologies still waiting to be spoken.
Maybe boundaries still need to be established.
Maybe control needs to be surrendered.
Maybe pride needs to die.
Maybe guilt has occupied a throne that belongs to grace.
Maybe you have punished yourself long enough for sins Jesus is calling you to confess and bring to His cross.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “This was sin. Bring it into the light. Repent. Come to Christ.”
Condemnation whispers, “You ruined everything. There is no hope. Keep hiding. Keep punishing yourself.”
The Gospel never asks you to pretend sin did not happen.
The Gospel does something far more astonishing.
It tells the truth about sin...
and then points toward a crucified and risen Savior greater than it.
That is our story.
Scandal to grace.
Failure to forgiveness.
Wandering to welcome.
Death to resurrection.
Not because parents rewrite everything.
Because Jesus does.
If this exposed guilt you have carried silently, do not hide behind a polished comment.
Be honest.
Somewhere, a parent who cried themselves to sleep last night may need to know that a chapter of rebellion is not necessarily the final chapter.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, consider staying close to this ministry.

If this ministry glorifies Christ, strengthens believers, and places biblical truth before people who are hurting, supporting that work is one tangible way you can participate in helping it continue and expand.
It is mission.
It is helping keep Scripture in front of people scrolling through despair.
It is helping put Christ-centered encouragement before a parent at 2:00 in the morning who thinks their child's rebellion means their entire life was a failure.
It is helping us keep creating, teaching, discipling, encouraging, warning, comforting, and pointing people toward Jesus.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help enormously.
One share costs nothing, but it may carry this truth into a home we could never reach ourselves.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker who is asking questions.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken families.
Because underneath all our parenting successes and parenting failures stands one truth every generation desperately needs:
Our children need Jesus.
Their parents need Jesus.
Their grandparents needed Jesus.
And the children who come after them will need Jesus.
So parent faithfully.
Repent honestly.
Love courageously.
Pray relentlessly.
Hold your children with open hands.
Refuse both crushing guilt and self-congratulating pride.
Plant.
Water.
Teach.
Correct.
Listen.
Apologize.
Forgive.
Pray.
And leave the throne to God.
Because one day you may discover that while you were begging God to rewrite your child's story, He was quietly rewriting yours too.
Your child's rebellion does not make Jesus powerless, and your child's obedience does not make you their savior. There has only ever been one Savior—and His name is Jesus Christ.
